results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate for parity-matching targets minus parity-mismatching targets; observed < null means the model over-commits to parity (odd/even) rules relative to people, observed > null means people use parity more.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate for parity-matching targets minus parity-mismatching targets; observed < null means the model over-commits to parity (odd/even) rules relative to people, observed > null means people use parity more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    par = np.mod(ex, 2)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    s = np.nansum(par, axis=1)
    alleven = s == 0; allodd = s == n
    uni = (alleven | allodd) & (n >= 2)
    setpar = np.where(allodd, 1.0, 0.0)
    match = uni & (np.mod(t, 2) == setpar)
    mis = uni & (np.mod(t, 2) != setpar)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if match.sum() == 0 or mis.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[match].mean() - r[mis].mean())

results.name: inside_vs_outside_range
results.description: Yes rate for targets strictly inside the [min,max] span of the examples minus yes rate for targets outside that span (sets with 2+ examples); observed > null means people treat the example range as a region more than the model does.
results.code:
# name: inside_vs_outside_range
# description: Yes rate for targets strictly inside the [min,max] span of the examples minus yes rate for targets outside that span (sets with 2+ examples); observed > null means people treat the example range as a region more than the model does.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    inside = (n >= 2) & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    outside = (n >= 2) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: near_far_similarity_gradient
results.description: Yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 15+ away from every example (excluding targets equal to an example); observed > null means people show more graded nearby-number generalization than the sharpened model produces.
results.code:
# name: near_far_similarity_gradient
# description: Yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 15+ away from every example (excluding targets equal to an example); observed > null means people show more graded nearby-number generalization than the sharpened model produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    near = (d >= 1) & (d <= 3)
    far = d >= 15
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: shared_last_digit_match
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all end in the same digit, yes rate for targets ending in that digit (and not equal to an example); observed < null means the model over-predicts generalization of "ends in d" rules, observed > null means it under-predicts.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_match
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all end in the same digit, yes rate for targets ending in that digit (and not equal to an example); observed < null means the model over-predicts generalization of "ends in d" rules, observed > null means it under-predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(ex, 10)
    first = ld[:, 0]
    same = np.all(np.isnan(ld) | (ld == first[:, None]), axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    isex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = same & (np.mod(t, 10) == first) & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials with trial_index >= 225 minus yes rate on trials with trial_index < 225; a nonzero observed value outside the null means a drift in yes-bias across the session that the stationary model does not produce (positive = people say yes more later).

results.name: lag1_response_dependence
results.description: P(yes | previous trial in the same session was yes) minus P(yes | previous was no), with sessions delimited by trial_index resets; observed > null means responses are sequentially perseverative, which the trial-independent model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: lag1_response_dependence
# description: P(yes | previous trial in the same session was yes) minus P(yes | previous was no), with sessions delimited by trial_index resets; observed > null means responses are sequentially perseverative, which the trial-independent model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    same = np.r_[False, ti[1:] > ti[:-1]]
    prev = np.r_[np.nan, r[:-1]]
    a = same & (prev == 1); b = same & (prev == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_set_response_variance
results.description: Mean over sets (with 10+ trials) of the Bernoulli variance p(1-p) of yes responses within the set; observed > null means people's answers within a set are less deterministic/more mixed than the sharpened all-or-none model predicts, observed < null more deterministic.

results.name: single_example_near_generalization
results.description: Yes rate for targets within 10 of the nearest example on 1-example sets minus the same on 4-example sets; observed > null means people loosen generalization with few examples more than the model's size principle implies (observed < null: less).
results.code:
# name: single_example_near_generalization
# description: Yes rate for targets within 10 of the nearest example on 1-example sets minus the same on 4-example sets; observed > null means people loosen generalization with few examples more than the model's size principle implies (observed < null: less).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = (n == 1) & (d >= 1) & (d <= 10)
    b = (n == 4) & (d >= 1) & (d <= 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
